summary: For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we created "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," an interactive field ledger of thirteen sites on the Moon and Mars where NASA hardware stopped moving and stayed, spanning 1967 to 2024. Users drag a time slider, pick a site, and discover what was left, why it stayed, and what it does today.We wanted to show that "abandoned" doesn't mean "forgotten." Our project tells three stories: traces of people (a family photo, golf balls), machines that outlived their plans (Viking, Spirit, Opportunity), and hardware that is still useful, like lunar laser reflectors and InSight's data. We linked to LROC, HiRISE, and NASA Trek so users can see the real sites.These objects are humanity's first footprints on other worlds. By making them visible and understandable, we help preserve exploration history, show that left-behind hardware often keeps delivering science, and invite everyone to connect with our shared space heritage.
details:
We built "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," an interactive field ledger of thirteen sites on the Moon and Mars where NASA hardware stopped moving and stayed. Users drag a slider through time, from 1967 to 2024, pick a site, and read what was left, why it stayed, and what it does today. The project turns scattered mission facts into one explorable story, so anyone can see what is still out there. It links to the original NASA sources, and we hope it helps people see left-behind hardware as shared exploration heritage, not space junk.

InSight's We built it with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using a range input for the time slider. We designed in Canva, took images and data from the NASA Science website, and hosted it on GitHub Pages. We tell the story three ways: traces of people, like a family photo and golf balls; machines that outlived their plans, like Viking, Spirit, and Opportunity; and silent hardware that is still useful, like laser reflectors and Insight's data.

We considered accuracy, rounding figures from NASA pages and treating coordinates as approximate; sources, so users can check the original data; audience, the public; and storytelling, favoring human stories over plain data lists.
